programs.nl_rule:
In the input, you should see...a large grid separated into two black section with a set of grey blocks in the middle.

The output grid size...is equal to the size of one of the original black section.

To make the output, you have to...take the right side section and turn it to the left rotating two times until all colored boxes start on the right.  The image will be the overlap of the two sides.

content.text:
Let me understand the rule. The grid is split by a vertical line of color 5 (divider). Near half is left of divider, far half is right. Fold far half over: reverse its columns. Then output = near where near != 0 else far.

Wait, let me check with the example.

Input is 10 rows, 9 columns. Divider at column 4 (0-indexed), value 5 everywhere. So near = columns 0..3 (4 wide), far = columns 5..8 reversed.

Far columns 5,6,7,8 reversed → column 8,7,6,5.

Row 0: far = [0,0,0,0] reversed = [0,0,0,0]. near=[0,0,0,0]. output row 0 = [0,0,0,0]. ✓

Row 2: near cols0-3 = [3,0,3,3]. far cols5-8 = [0,0,3,0] reversed = [0,3,0,0]. output = near!=0? 3, else far: [3, 0==0→far=3? wait let's compute cell by cell.

near = [3,0,3,3], far reversed = [0,3,0,0].
cell0: near=3→3. cell1: near=0→far=3. cell2: near=3→3. cell3: near=3→3. output=[3,3,3,3]. ✓ matches.

Row 3: near cols0-3 = [0,0,0,2]. far cols5-8=[0,0,0,0] reversed=[0,0,0,0]. output=[0,0,0,2]. ✓

Great.

Now let me think about how to teach the student. I should show one or two examples with show_transformed_input (which gives gold automatically). Actually I could use show_example with the teacher example, but I need to author it correctly. Better to use show_transformed_input so gold is computed.

But careful: the verifier requires grid conventions. Input must have a divider (solid line). Input conventions: a solid line of one colour splits the picture. Let me just provide varied examples.

Let me design an input grid with a vertical divider, non-square sizes, to demonstrate folding.

Actually, I should be efficient. Let me give a couple of demonstrations via show_transformed_input, perhaps also a query_student to check, then start exam.

The exam is held-out generator inputs. Likely similar structure. The rule: fold far half onto near half. Output size = one half. Which is "near" vs "far"? In the rule text it says "take the right side section and turn it to the left rotating two times until all colored boxes start on the right. The image will be the overlap of the two sides." That's 180 rotation. But the verifier uses mirror fold (reverse columns). Hmm, the natural language says rotate two times (180 degrees), but the verifier does mirror about vertical line. For a 180 rotation, you'd reverse both rows and columns. The verifier only reverses columns (horizontal mirror). Interesting discrepancy. We must follow the verifier since that's what grades.

Actually wait - "turn it to the left rotating two times" - rotating the right half 180° and placing... hmm. But verifier is definitive. Let's just match verifier: fold = mirror columns.

Let me verify more carefully with row 6: near cols0-3=[3,3,3,0]. far cols5-8=[3,3,3,3] reversed=[3,3,3,3]. output = [3,3,3,3]. Given output row 6 = [3,3,3,3]. ✓

Row 7: near=[0,0,0,3], far cols5-8=[3,0,0,0] reversed=[0,0,0,3]. output = cell3: near=3→3; others near=0→far: cell0 far=0, cell1=0, cell2=0. output=[0,0,0,3]. ✓

Good.

Now design demonstrations. I'll provide a small grid with vertical divider.

Let me make a 4x5 grid: divider column 2. Near cols 0-1, far cols 3-4.

Example A:
Input:
row0: [0,0,7,0,0]
row1: [1,0,7,0,2]
row2: [0,1,7,3,0]
row3: [0,0,7,0,0]

Hmm, need something meaningful. Near cols0-1, far cols3-4 reversed = cols [4,3].

row0: near=[0,0], far=[0,0]→[0,0]; out [0,0]
row1: near=[1,0], far=[2,0]→[0,2]; out: cell0:1, cell1: near0→far=0... wait far reversed: original far row = [0,2] (cols3,4). reversed = [2,0]. So out cell0: near=1→1. cell1: near=0→far=0. out=[1,0]. Hmm okay.

Let me just make it and let environment compute. I'll give a couple.

Actually the important thing is teaching the rule. The student learns from demonstrations. Let me provide two demonstrations with different sizes/orientations (vertical divider and maybe horizontal divider?) The verifier also handles horizontal divider (odd rows). But natural language mentions "two black sections" and "grey blocks in the middle" - likely vertical divider. The generator probably produces vertical dividers mostly. But could include horizontal. Hmm.

The task says input has large grid separated into two black sections with grey blocks in middle. Divider color 5 in example. But verifier reads divider color off grid. Let me not overthink.

Let me give demos with vertical divider (the likely case) and one query.

I think giving 2 transformations should suffice. Let me pick inputs.

Demo 1 (vertical divider, size 5 wide):
Input:
[0,4,0,5,0]
[4,0,0,5,0]
[0,0,4,5,4]
[0,4,0,5,0]

Wait divider must be a full column of same colour. Column 3 = 5 all rows? columns index: 0,1,2 near; 3 divider; 4 far. near cols0-2, far col4. Reversed far = same.

row0: near=[0,4,0], far=[0]; out=[0,4,0]
row1: near=[4,0,0], far=[0]; out=[4,0,0]
row2: near=[0,0,4], far=[4]; out=[0,0,4]
row3: near=[0,4,0], far=[0]; out=[0,4,0]

Boring. Let me make wider far half.

Demo 1: width 7, divider col3. Near cols0-2, far cols4-6.

Input rows (4 rows):
row0: [0,0,0,5,1,2,3]  → far reversed [3,2,1]
row1: [4,0,0,5,0,0,0]  → far [0,0,0]
row2: [0,5... 

Hmm wait near must have some ink. Let me craft:
row0: [0,0,0,5,1,2,3] → near [0,0,0], far rev [3,2,1] → out [3,2,1]
row1: [4,0,0,5,0,5,0]... 

Let me keep it simple but instructive:
Input:
[0,0,0,5,1,2,3]
[4,4,0,5,0,0,0]
[0,0,4,5,0,0,4]
[0,0,0,5,0,0,0]

near:
r0 [0,0,0], r1 [4,4,0], r2 [0,0,4], r3 [0,0,0]
far original cols4-6:
r0 [1,2,3], r1 [0,0,0], r2 [0,0,4], r3 [0,0,0]
far reversed:
r0 [3,2,1], r1 [0,0,0], r2 [4,0,0], r3 [0,0,0]
out:
r0 [3,2,1]
r1 [4,4,0]
r2 [4,0,4]  (cell0 near0→far4, cell1 near0→far0, cell2 near4→4)
r3 [0,0,0]

That demonstrates well.

I'll use show_transformed_input so gold is computed. Actually show_transformed_input fills gold and shows pair to student. Good.

Let me do 2-3 calls. Since I can't verify my hand calc, using show_transformed_input is safe.

Also maybe show a horizontal-divider example? Not sure generator produces those. The rule mentions "two black section" plural with grey in middle. Likely vertical. I'll include one horizontal just in case? Might confuse. Hmm.

Actually the verifier: if w is even but has horizontal divider (h odd), it folds rows. The generator "e3497940" typical ARC task folds along the divider whichever orientation. Held-out inputs could be either. To teach robustness, include one horizontal example too.

Let me create horizontal example: divider row is a full row of same color. E.g. 5 columns, 5 rows, divider row 2.

Input:
[0,1,0,0,0]
[0,0,0,2,0]
[5,5,5,5,5]
[0,0,0,0,3]
[0,4,0,0,0]

near = rows0-1: [[0,1,0,0,0],[0,0,0,2,0]]
far = rows3-4 reversed (row4 then row3):
[[0,4,0,0,0],[0,0,0,0,3]]
out:
row0: near[0,1,0,0,0]; far[0,4,0,0,0] → cell by cell: [0→0? near0=0→far=0, near1=1→1, near0→0, near0→0, near0→0] = [0,1,0,0,0]
row1: near[0,0,0,2,0]; far[0,0,0,0,3] → [0,0,0,2,3]

Good demonstration that folding also works horizontally and that far half is reversed in row order.

I'll show both vertical and horizontal examples.

But wait—maybe including horizontal could mislead if the exam only has vertical? No, the verifier handles both, and the student generalizes. Actually teaching both is safer.

Let me also do a query_student to check understanding before exam. Query gives me student's prediction and gold. That helps me decide if more teaching needed. But it also costs. Let's do 2 demos + 1 query.

Let me start with show_transformed_input for vertical demo.

Let me reconsider: the output must be the shape of one half - which half? The near (left) half. The rule says output size equals one of the black sections. Yes near half.

Let me proceed.

Call 1: show_transformed_input vertical.
Call 2: show_transformed_input horizontal.
Call 3: query_student with a new vertical input.

Actually I can do calls 1 and 2 in parallel, then query.

Let me craft the query input to test edge: near and far both have ink, some overlap.

Query input (width 7, divider col3, 4 rows):
[1,0,0,5,0,0,2]
[0,2,0,5,0,3,0]
[0,0,3,5,4,0,0]
[0,0,0,5,0,0,0]

near: r0[1,0,0],r1[0,2,0],r2[0,0,3],r3[0,0,0]
far cols4-6 original: r0[0,0,2],r1[0,3,0],r2[4,0,0],r3[0,0,0]
far reversed: r0[2,0,0],r1[0,3,0],r2[0,0,4],r3[0,0,0]
out: r0[1,0,2]? cell0 near1→1, cell1 near0→far0, cell2 near0→far0? wait far reversed r0 = [2,0,0]. cell2 far=0. So [1,0,0]? Let me recompute: far original r0 = cols4,5,6 = [0,0,2]. reversed = [2,0,0]. So index0→2, index1→0, index2→0.
out r0: cell0 near=1→1; cell1 near=0→far=0; cell2 near=0→far=0 → [1,0,0].
r1: near[0,2,0], far rev [0,3,0] → [0,2,0]? cell0 near0→far0; cell1 near2→2; cell2 near0→far0 → [0,2,0].
r2: near[0,0,3], far orig[4,0,0] rev[0,0,4] → cell0 near0→far0; cell1 near0→far0; cell2 near3→3 → [0,0,3].
r3 [0,0,0].

Hmm that's not very informative. Whatever, the query just probes.

OK let's just go. I'll trust environment for gold.

Actually, let me just do demonstrations; the query isn't strictly necessary but good to confirm. I'll include one query.

tools.name: show_example

input_grid.description: Rectangular matrix; each cell is an integer color 0–9.

output_grid.description: Rectangular matrix; each cell is an integer color 0–9.

tools.description: Show the Student a labeled input-output pair that you authored. If your output matches the rule, the pair is shown and you receive a success acknowledgement only. If it does not match, the pair is not shown and you receive the gold output so you can correct it.

tools.name: show_transformed_input

input_grid.description: Rectangular matrix; each cell is an integer color 0–9.

tools.description: Provide only an input grid. The environment applies the verifier and shows the resulting gold input-output pair to the student.

tools.name: query_student

input_grid.description: Rectangular matrix; each cell is an integer color 0–9.

tools.description: Probe the student with an input of your choice. You receive the student's predicted output, the gold output, and whether they matched. The student does not see the gold pair unless you later show it with show_example or show_transformed_input.

tools.name: start_exam
tools.description: End teaching and send the student to the exam: they must solve held-out generator inputs (unseen in demonstrations or probes) with the history so far. No further teaching after this.

content.text: Both matched my predictions. Let me do a query to check student understanding.
